sentences.text: Vulcanodon was a relatively small sauropod, reaching only about 11 meters in length compared to its larger relatives.
In 2010, Gregory S. Paul estimated that this animal weighed roughly 3.5 tonnes.
Its sturdy, pillar-like legs had forelimbs that reached 76 percent of the length of the hindlimbs.
The skeleton included a sacrum formed by four fused vertebrae, a feature distinguishing it from earlier prosauropods which had only three.
The first bone was unearthed by B. A. Gibson in July 1969 during excavations in Zimbabwe.
Michael Raath formally named and described the genus in 1972.
The remains were recovered from the Vulcanodon beds, a sediment unit inside the Batoka Formation made mostly of flood basalts.
Initially, researchers believed the animal might have been omnivorous because knife-shaped teeth found nearby suggested a varied diet.
Later studies revealed those sharp teeth actually belonged to a different theropod predator that scavenged the carcass.
Raath hypothesized in 1972 that the presence of these carnivorous teeth near the pelvis indicated the body was in a death pose with the neck bent backward.
However, Cooper argued in 1984 that the teeth were not part of Vulcanodon but came from a theropod scavenger.
This finding suggested that the large size of sauropods did not evolve as an adaptation to living in water.
Vulcanodon and Tazoudasaurus were united in this family, although this grouping is not universally accepted.
It remains debated whether the close relationship between Tazoudasaurus and Vulcanodon is confirmed, as other analyses failed to verify it.
The animal lived during the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic.
The total time range for the species spans from 199.5 to 184.2 million years ago.
